overview.title: 📖 Overview: What Exact Words Make a Substitute?
overview.subtitle: Temurah 26a–26b
overview.hebrewSource: תַּחַת זוֹ, תְּמוּרַת זוֹ, חֲלִיפַת זוֹ — הֲרֵי זוֹ תְּמוּרָה
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: Rabbi Yoḥanan clarifies exactly where Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosei's dispute lives: everyone agrees that explicit sequential language ('this takes effect, then this') follows the first statement, and explicit conditional language ('this only if that too') gives both — the argument is only about ambiguous back-to-back phrasing like the mishna's own case. A series of baraitot test this through half-burnt/half-peace and half-burnt/half-sin offering declarations, revealing that Rabbi Meir's rule is really about which phrase came first, not about sin-offering sanctity mixing freely. Rabbi Yoḥanan's case of two partners consecrating their respective halves at different times yields three important principles about deferred sanctity. Abaye then raises (and partly leaves unresolved) a further dilemma about mixing substitute-status with animal-tithe status. The daf closes with a new mishna cataloging exactly which Hebrew phrases create a valid substitute and which merely describe ordinary redemption.

slides.title: 🗣️ Where Everyone Agrees, and Where the Real Dispute Lives
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Yoḥanan narrows the Rabbi Meir/Rabbi Yosei disagreement to one ambiguous phrasing

lines.speaker: Explicit sequence
lines.text: 'This will take effect [as substitute for the burnt offering], and AFTERWARD this will take effect [for the peace offering]' — everyone agrees: only the FIRST sanctity takes effect.

lines.speaker: Explicit condition
lines.text: 'This won't take effect UNLESS that also takes effect' — everyone agrees: BOTH sanctities take effect together.

lines.speaker: The disputed case
lines.text: But what about the mishna's actual wording — 'the substitute of the burnt offering, the substitute of the peace offering' — with no explicit sequence OR condition stated?

lines.speaker: Rabbi Meir
lines.text: Since he didn't say 'and,' this reads like implicit SEQUENCE — only the first phrase (burnt offering) takes effect.

lines.speaker: Rabbi Yosei
lines.text: He avoided 'and' precisely because he WANTED both — saying 'and' would have implied a half-and-half split, which he mistakenly thought couldn't be sacrificed at all.

callout.label: The insight:
callout.text: Both sages agree on the clear cases; they disagree only about how to read genuinely ambiguous back-to-back phrasing — a matter of interpreting silence, not explicit words.

slides.title: 🔀 Testing the Rule With Half-Burnt/Half-X Declarations
slides.subtitle: The pattern of agreement reveals what Rabbi Meir's rule REALLY means
rows: 'Half burnt offering, half peace offering' (as temurah)
All sacrificed as burnt offering (first phrase wins)
Grazes, sold, split proceeds fund each offering
Both take effect — but a sin offering can never be 'half,' so the WHOLE animal dies
'Half SIN offering, half burnt offering' (sin offering spoken FIRST)
Even Rabbi Meir agrees: the animal dies

callout.label: Why the last row matters:
callout.text: This agreement proves Rabbi Meir's rule is genuinely about WHICH PHRASE CAME FIRST — not (as one might otherwise think) about sin-offering sanctity being uniquely able to 'absorb' a mixed designation.

slides.title: 🤝 Two Partners, One Animal — Three Lessons
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Yoḥanan's case: consecrating half now, the other half later

steps.content: 1️⃣ Case: two partners jointly own an animal. One consecrates HIS half; later, he buys out the OTHER half and consecrates that too. Now the whole animal is consecrated — but it can NEVER be sacrificed
2️⃣ Lesson one: value-sanctity (קְדוּשַּׁת דָּמִים) alone — like consecrating just half an animal — is enough to permanently DEFER it from ever reaching the altar
3️⃣ Lesson two: even a LIVING animal (not just one already slaughtered) can become permanently disqualified through such deferral
4️⃣ Lesson three: deferral that happens right at the START (the very moment of consecration) counts as real, permanent deferral — just as much as deferral that happens later

callout.label: Ripple effect:
callout.text: Because the animal itself can never be sacrificed, even its SUBSTITUTE inherits that same permanent limitation — it too can only graze until blemished.

nodes.content: ✅ Clear case: 'half burnt offering, half animal tithe' — EVERYONE agrees the burnt offering wins entirely, since tithe-sanctity only comes from passing animals under the rod, which isn't happening here at all
❓ Harder case: 'half SUBSTITUTE, half animal tithe' — substitute-sanctity doesn't apply either (no consecrated animal was standing before him for substitution)

🔀 Does 'substitute' win, since it applies broadly to ALL consecrated categories? Or does 'tithe' win, since tithe-consecration is uniquely powerful (even catching the animal counted BEFORE and AFTER the actual tenth)?

callout.label: Why the difference:
callout.text: Unlike the clear-cut burnt-offering case, here NEITHER named sanctity technically applies at all — making the comparison genuinely uncertain.

slides.title: 📜 New Mishna: The Exact Words That Create a Substitute
slides.subtitle: Testing 'תַּחַת' against a seemingly contradictory baraita

lines.speaker: Mishna
lines.text: 'This is IN PLACE OF that' (תַּחַת), 'the SUBSTITUTE of that,' or 'the EXCHANGE for that' — all three create a valid substitute. But 'this is DESACRALIZED ONTO that' (מְחוּלֶּלֶת) does NOT.

lines.speaker: Contradicting baraita
lines.text: For bedek habayit (Temple upkeep) items — which can never generate a substitute — 'exchange' and 'substitute' language accomplish NOTHING. But 'תַּחַת' and 'מְחוּלֶּלֶת' DO work — as ordinary desacralization/redemption!

lines.speaker: The puzzle
lines.text: If 'תַּחַת' always means SUBSTITUTION (as the mishna implies), how can the same word also work for bedek habayit, where substitution is impossible?

lines.speaker: Abaye's resolution
lines.text: 'תַּחַת' is genuinely AMBIGUOUS — sometimes it means associating one sanctity with another (substitution), and sometimes it simply means desacralization/redemption. Context (and which type of consecrated item is involved) determines which sense applies.

callout.label: Why this matters:
callout.text: The mishna's precise vocabulary for temurah isn't purely mechanical — the same Hebrew word can carry two different legal meanings depending on what kind of consecrated item stands opposite it.

summary.principle: The Rabbi Meir/Rabbi Yosei dispute is really about how to read ambiguous back-to-back phrasing (not explicit sequence or condition), value-sanctity alone can permanently defer even a living animal from the altar, and the word 'תַּחַת' itself carries two different legal meanings depending on context.

flowSteps.content: 🗣️ Everyone agrees on explicit sequence/condition; the real dispute is only ambiguous phrasing like the mishna's own
🔀 Half-and-half baraitot confirm: Rabbi Meir's rule is genuinely 'first phrase wins,' not special sin-offering logic

columns.content: 🤝 Two-partners case: value-sanctity alone permanently defers a living animal

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: substitution requires the right words in the right context — 'תַּחַת' means either association or mere redemption, depending on what stands opposite it

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Yoḥanan, in what case do Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosei both agree that only the FIRST sanctity takes effect?
o: Whenever any two sanctities are mentioned at all
When the speaker explicitly says 'this shall take effect, and AFTERWARD this shall take effect' — clear stated sequence
Never — they always disagree
Only for sin offerings
quiz.e: Rabbi Yoḥanan clarifies that explicit sequential language is agreed upon by all; the real dispute concerns only ambiguous phrasing like the mishna's 'substitute of the burnt offering, substitute of the peace offering' with no explicit sequence stated.

quiz.q: What does the baraita's agreement — that saying 'half sin offering, half burnt offering' (sin offering FIRST) always results in death — prove about Rabbi Meir's reasoning?
o: That Rabbi Meir never really holds his stated position
That his rule is genuinely about which phrase was spoken FIRST, not about sin-offering sanctity being uniquely able to absorb a mixed designation
That sin offerings can always be split in half
Nothing significant
quiz.e: Since even Rabbi Meir agrees the animal dies when sin offering is named first, this confirms his general rule is 'the first-stated designation wins' — not some special rule about sin-offering sanctity 'catching' a mixed case.

quiz.q: What three halakhic lessons does the Gemara derive from Rabbi Yoḥanan's case of two partners consecrating their respective halves of an animal at different times?
o: Nothing of significance; it's a marginal case
Value-sanctity alone can permanently defer an animal; even a LIVING animal can be permanently disqualified; deferral at the very outset counts as real deferral
Only that partners can never own consecrated animals together
That temurah never applies to jointly-owned animals
quiz.e: The Gemara draws three lessons: value-sanctity (from consecrating just half) is enough to permanently defer an animal, living (not just slaughtered) animals can be permanently disqualified, and deferral from the very start of consecration counts as genuine deferral.

quiz.q: What is the outcome of Abaye's dilemma about declaring 'half substitute, half animal tithe' for a non-sacred animal?
o: The substitute-status always wins
The tithe-status always wins
The dilemma is left unresolved as teiku, since neither named sanctity technically applies to the situation at all
The animal is automatically non-sacred
quiz.e: Unlike the clear-cut 'half burnt offering, half tithe' case (where burnt offering plainly wins since tithe-consecration requires passing animals under a rod), the substitute/tithe case has neither sanctity technically applying, leaving the Gemara's dilemma unresolved.

quiz.q: How does Abaye resolve the apparent contradiction between the mishna (where 'תַּחַת' creates a substitute) and a baraita (where 'תַּחַת' works for bedek habayit items, which can never generate a substitute)?
o: He says one of the two sources must be wrong
He explains that 'תַּחַת' is genuinely ambiguous — it can mean either associating one sanctity with another (substitution) or simple desacralization/redemption, depending on context
He says bedek habayit items don't really exist
He rejects the mishna's ruling entirely
quiz.e: Abaye resolves the contradiction by showing that the word 'תַּחַת' carries two distinct possible meanings — substitution-language in one context, redemption-language in another — so both sources can be correct without contradiction.
